patient.name: Kwabena Mensah
patient.setting: Emergency Department, then neurosurgical high-dependency unit
patient.complaint: Three weeks of worsening morning headaches and vomiting, now drowsy
background: Non-small cell lung cancer diagnosed 8 months ago, on follow-up
Retired bus driver from Lewisham, lives with his wife

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with morning headache worse on coughing, vomiting and papilloedema, or a young woman with a high BMI (IIH). Cushing's triad and a 6th nerve palsy are the classic signs to spot.

points: Three weeks of headaches, **worst on waking**.
Worse when he coughs or bends to tie his shoes.
Vomits most mornings; double vision for 4 days.

steps.lead: Kwabena's skull holds a growing **space-occupying lesion** until the pressure rises: a tumour is one of the commonest causes of raised ICP.
Morning headache worse on coughing, vomiting, diplopia and a dropping GCS: Kwabena has the **classic raised ICP picture**.

points: Fundoscopy: **both optic discs swollen**, margins blurred.
Left eye **cannot abduct**: horizontal double vision on looking left.
Pupils equal and reactive for now.

steps.q: Kwabena's left eye cannot look outwards. Which nerve is affected?
steps.r: The **abducens nerve** has a long intracranial course, so it is stretched by raised ICP: a 'false localising sign' rather than a lesion at the nerve.

steps.text: **Bilateral papilloedema** + headache worse lying, coughing or straining = raised ICP until proven otherwise. A **6th nerve palsy** is the cranial nerve sign it causes.

steps.lead: Kwabena's cause is a tumour. The other face of raised ICP in the exam is **IIH**: a young woman with a high BMI or on lithium, with a normal scan.

steps.title: Two exam pictures of raised ICP
head: Feature
Space-occupying lesion
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension
rows: Papilloedema, visual blurring, CN VI palsy

points: Overnight in ED, Kwabena becomes harder to rouse.
BP climbs to **196/92**; pulse falls to **48**.

steps.text: Rising BP with a falling pulse and GCS is **Cushing's triad** forming: a late, pre-herniation sign.

steps.lead: Kwabena now has **hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing** with a widening pulse pressure: he is close to herniating.

steps.text: Do not treat Cushing's triad as a 'hypertensive emergency' with antihypertensives. The BP is rising to **keep the brain perfused**; treat the ICP.

steps.lead: A junior suggests an LP to rule out meningitis. With papilloedema and possible SOL, that could **cone** Kwabena: scan first.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' with the answer urgent CT head, and the trap of lumbar puncture before imaging. In IIH, the LP opening pressure confirms the diagnosis once imaging is clear.

steps.q: Kwabena has papilloedema and a falling GCS. Which investigation first?
steps.r: **Urgent CT head** quickly shows a SOL, bleed or hydrocephalus. LP before imaging risks fatal brainstem herniation.

steps.lead: Kwabena's CT is done within the hour. It shows exactly the pattern of a **cerebral metastasis**.

points: CT head: **hypodense lesion** in the right frontoparietal lobe.
Midline shifted 7 mm to the left.

steps.title: Bloods on arrival
steps.text: Bloods exclude metabolic causes of drowsiness (sodium, calcium, glucose) but do not explain his signs.

steps.lead: LP gives the **opening pressure**, the gold standard for raised CSF pressure, but for Kwabena it stays off the table: his CT shows a mass with shift.

steps.title: Investigating suspected raised ICP
nodes: Suspect raised ICP (headache, papilloedema, falling GCS)
Lesion, bleed or hydrocephalus → treat cause
CT normal → MR/CT venography (venous sinus thrombosis?)
steps.caption: Imaging always comes before the needle.

visual.title: CSF opening pressure (lying on side)
visual.label: Typical IIH 34
visual.caption: In IIH, CT is normal and the LP opening pressure is high (above 25 cmH2O in adults).

steps.lead: If Kwabena's CT had been normal, **MR/CT venography** would look for venous sinus thrombosis. On the neuro unit, MRI and an ICP monitor follow.

steps.text: 'Fundoscopy' shows papilloedema but does not identify the cause. When asked for the **initial investigation** in suspected raised ICP, choose **CT head**.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': head up 30 degrees, IV mannitol while awaiting theatre, and high-dose dexamethasone when the cause is a tumour with oedema. Hyperventilation is a temporary rescue.

steps.lead: Kwabena's GCS is 10 with Cushing's triad: **ABCDE**, oxygen and an immediate call to the neurosurgical registrar and ICU.

steps.q: While the neurosurgeon is on the way, what is the first simple measure?
steps.r: **Head elevation to 30 degrees** improves cerebral venous drainage and lowers ICP. Lying flat or head-down raises ICP.

steps.lead: Kwabena is sat **30 degrees head-up** and given **IV 20% mannitol** while theatre is arranged.
His raised ICP comes from a metastasis with **vasogenic oedema**, so he also gets **high-dose IV dexamethasone**.

steps.text: **Dexamethasone** works for tumour oedema (vasogenic). It is **not** used for raised ICP after head injury or bleeding: those get mannitol and surgery.

points: Two hours later his left pupil starts to dilate.
Anaesthetist intubates him for airway protection.
Ventilated to a slightly low CO2 as a bridge to theatre.

steps.lead: Kwabena's **controlled hyperventilation** buys time only. Osmotherapy continues and neurosurgery decompresses the lesion.

visual.title: Target PaCO2 during controlled hyperventilation
visual.label: Kwabena 4.3 kPa
visual.caption: A slightly low CO2 shrinks cerebral blood volume; too low starves the brain of blood.

steps.title: Emergency management of raised ICP
nodes: ABCDE, oxygen, senior + neuro + ICU help
Definitive: treat cause (surgery, CSF diversion, antibiotics)

steps.lead: NICE head injury guidance and IIH guidance frame how these patients are scanned and escalated; Kwabena's care follows the same CT-first, escalate-early logic.

science.exam: Science questions ask the mechanism: Monro-Kellie, CPP = MAP − ICP, why Cushing's triad causes bradycardia, how mannitol or hyperventilation lowers ICP, or why LP causes coning.

steps.lead: Kwabena's tumour and oedema took up space; his CSF and venous blood were squeezed out until there was **no reserve left**.

steps.text: Flat while CSF and blood are displaced, then **steep**: once compensation is exhausted, small extra volume causes a big rise in ICP.

steps.q: Kwabena's MAP is 95 mmHg and his ICP is 35 mmHg. What is his CPP?
steps.r: **CPP = MAP − ICP** = 95 − 35 = 60 mmHg. Rising ICP lowers CPP unless MAP rises too.

steps.lead: Kwabena's falling CPP drove a **sympathetic BP surge**; baroreceptors then slowed his heart, and brainstem compression made his breathing irregular.
The mannitol Kwabena received pulled water out of his brain into the blood along an **osmotic gradient**.
His low CO2 on the ventilator caused **cerebral vasoconstriction**, but too much would have made his brain ischaemic.
Draining CSF from Kwabena's spine would have dropped pressure below the foramen magnum and pulled his brainstem down: **coning**.

steps.text: Mannitol and hyperventilation both lower ICP, but by different routes: **mannitol = osmosis (water out)**, **hyperventilation = vasoconstriction (blood volume down)**.

mcq.q: Which three features make up Cushing's triad?
mcq.r: **Hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing**: a late sign of severe raised ICP and herniation risk.

mcq.q: Which cranial nerve palsy is classically caused by raised ICP?
mcq.r: The **abducens (CN VI)** nerve is stretched by raised ICP: a false localising sign.

mcq.q: Who is classically affected by idiopathic intracranial hypertension?
o: Young women with a high BMI
mcq.r: IIH: **young women with a high BMI**, or regular lithium use.

mcq.q: When is a raised ICP headache classically worst?
mcq.r: **Morning headaches**, worse on coughing, straining and bending.

mcq.q: What is the first-line investigation for suspected raised ICP?
mcq.r: **Urgent CT head** identifies a SOL, hydrocephalus or bleed.

mcq.q: Why must CT come before lumbar puncture in suspected raised ICP?
o: LP is less sensitive than CT
mcq.r: With a SOL, LP can cause fatal **brainstem herniation (coning)**.

mcq.q: After a normal CT head, which test excludes venous sinus thrombosis?
mcq.r: **MR/CT venography** looks for venous outflow obstruction.

mcq.q: What is the first-line pharmacological treatment for raised ICP awaiting definitive treatment?
Which steroid is used for raised ICP from a brain tumour?
How does controlled hyperventilation lower ICP?
o: Draws water out of brain tissue
mcq.r: Lower **PaCO2 → cerebral vasoconstriction** → less cerebral blood volume.

prompts.q: What is raised ICP and what are its common causes?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: think of the three things in the skull and what can add volume.

points.p: Abnormal rise in pressure in the cranial vault from extra brain tissue, blood or CSF
points.why: Any extra volume in a rigid skull raises pressure.

points.p: Tumour / space-occupying lesion
points.why: Classic exam stem: known cancer plus morning headache.

points.p: Intracranial haemorrhage
points.why: Extradural or subdural after trauma are typical.

points.p: Hydrocephalus
points.why: Treated with CSF diversion.

points.p: Cerebral oedema and CNS infection or abscess
points.why: Abscess needs urgent antibiotics and often drainage.

prompts.q: What are the classic symptoms and signs of raised ICP?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the headache pattern plus papilloedema is the stem; the CN VI palsy is the detail.

points.p: Morning headache, worse coughing, straining or bending
points.why: Lying flat overnight and CO2 retention in sleep raise ICP.

points.p: Nausea and vomiting
points.why: Often worse in the morning too.

points.p: Bilateral papilloedema
points.why: Seen on fundoscopy as blurred optic disc margins.

points.p: Abducens (CN VI) palsy with diplopia
points.why: False localising sign: the nerve is stretched, not the lesion site.

points.p: Reduced GCS, confusion, seizures, abnormal pupils
points.why: A dilating pupil suggests uncal herniation compressing CN III.

prompts.q: What is Cushing's triad and what does it tell you?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: a high BP with a slow pulse in a drowsy patient is the brain, not the heart.

points.p: Hypertension (widening pulse pressure)
points.why: The BP rises to protect CPP.

points.p: Bradycardia
points.why: Baroreceptor reflex response to the BP surge.

points.p: Irregular breathing
points.why: From brainstem compression.

points.p: Late sign: poor prognosis, imminent herniation
points.why: Needs immediate neurosurgical and ICU escalation.

prompts.q: Which patient gets idiopathic intracranial hypertension and how does it present?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: young, female, high BMI, headache and papilloedema with a normal CT.

points.p: Young woman with a high BMI
points.why: The most common exam stem for raised ICP without a lesion.

points.p: Regular lithium use
points.why: A drug cause to recognise in the history.

points.p: Headache with papilloedema and visual blurring
points.why: Untreated, it can cause permanent visual loss.

prompts.q: Why is lumbar puncture dangerous in raised ICP, and when is it safe?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: any stem with papilloedema or a falling GCS and an LP option is a trap.

points.p: Can cause brainstem herniation through the foramen magnum (coning)
points.why: Often fatal.

points.p: Contraindicated until CT has excluded a SOL
points.why: CT first, then LP only if safe.

prompts.q: What is the first-line investigation, what is the gold standard, and what comes next if CT is normal?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: 'initial' = CT head; 'confirms raised CSF pressure' = LP opening pressure, after CT.

points.p: Urgent CT head first-line
points.why: Rapidly shows SOL, bleed or hydrocephalus.

points.p: Metastasis: hypodense lesion with surrounding oedema
points.why: Ring enhancement with contrast is common in metastases and abscess.

points.p: LP opening pressure is the gold standard for raised CSF pressure
points.why: Used to confirm IIH once imaging is normal.

points.p: MR/CT venography to exclude venous sinus thrombosis
points.why: Venous sinus thrombosis can mimic IIH.

points.p: MRI brain, bloods and ICP monitoring in ICU
points.why: Monitoring guides treatment on the neuro unit.

prompts.q: What are the immediate steps in managing raised ICP, in order?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: 'first step' = positioning; 'first-line drug' = mannitol.

points.p: ABCDE with urgent senior, neurosurgical and ICU help
points.why: Intubate if GCS 8 or less to protect the airway.

points.p: Head elevation to 30 degrees
points.why: Improves venous drainage from the brain.

points.p: IV 20% mannitol (osmotic diuretic) while awaiting theatre
points.why: Hypertonic saline is the alternative osmotherapy.

points.p: Controlled hyperventilation in severe cases
points.why: Temporary bridge only; risks ischaemia.

points.p: Neurosurgical intervention / treat the cause
points.why: The definitive fix.

prompts.q: How is the underlying cause of raised ICP treated?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: match the steroid to the tumour; never to a bleed.

points.p: Tumour: high-dose IV dexamethasone + neurosurgical review
points.why: Reduces vasogenic oedema around tumours.

points.p: Bleed: neurosurgical or stroke pathway
points.why: Extradural haematoma needs urgent evacuation.

points.p: Hydrocephalus: CSF diversion
points.why: External ventricular drain or VP shunt.

points.p: Infection or abscess: urgent treatment (antibiotics, drainage)
points.why: Do not delay antibiotics in suspected CNS infection.

prompts.q: What is the Monro-Kellie doctrine and how does it relate to CPP?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: fixed box, three contents, CPP = MAP − ICP.

points.p: Skull is a rigid fixed volume containing brain, blood and CSF
points.why: So volumes must trade off.

points.p: A rise in one must be offset by a fall in another, or ICP rises
points.why: CSF and venous blood are displaced first.

points.p: Once compensation is exhausted, ICP rises steeply
points.why: Why patients can deteriorate suddenly.

points.p: CPP = MAP − ICP
points.why: Rising ICP lowers CPP unless MAP rises.

prompts.q: How do mannitol, hyperventilation and dexamethasone each lower ICP?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: water, blood and oedema: one drug for each.

points.p: Mannitol: osmotic gradient draws water out of brain into vessels
points.why: Temporary effect.

points.p: Hyperventilation: low CO2 causes cerebral vasoconstriction, less blood volume
points.why: Short-lived and can cause ischaemia.

points.p: Dexamethasone: reduces vasogenic oedema around tumours
points.why: Not for traumatic brain injury.

glossary.ICP: Intracranial pressure: the pressure inside the skull, normally about 5 to 15 mmHg in adults.
glossary.CPP: Cerebral perfusion pressure: MAP minus ICP; the pressure driving blood through the brain.
glossary.MAP: Mean arterial pressure: the average arterial pressure over one cardiac cycle.
glossary.Monro-Kellie doctrine: The skull is a fixed box of brain, blood and CSF, so a rise in one must be offset by another.
glossary.Papilloedema: Swelling of both optic discs caused by raised intracranial pressure, seen on fundoscopy as blurred disc margins.
glossary.Fundoscopy: Looking at the back of the eye with an ophthalmoscope to see the optic disc, vessels and retina.
glossary.Abducens: The sixth cranial nerve, which moves the eye outwards; often stretched by raised ICP.
glossary.False localising sign: A sign caused by raised pressure in general, not by a lesion at that site, such as a 6th nerve palsy.
glossary.Cushing's triad: Hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing: a late sign of severe raised ICP before herniation.
glossary.Pulse pressure: Systolic minus diastolic blood pressure; it widens in Cushing's triad.
glossary.Baroreceptor: Pressure sensors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch that slow the heart when BP rises.
glossary.Herniation: Brain tissue pushed out of its normal compartment by pressure, compressing vital structures.
glossary.Coning: Downward herniation of the brainstem and cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum; often fatal.
glossary.Foramen magnum: The large hole at the base of the skull through which the brainstem joins the spinal cord.
glossary.SOL: Space-occupying lesion: a mass such as a tumour, abscess or haematoma that takes up room in the skull.
glossary.IIH: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension: raised CSF pressure with no lesion, typically in young women with a high BMI.
glossary.CSF: Cerebrospinal fluid: clear fluid around the brain and spinal cord.
glossary.Hydrocephalus: Build-up of CSF in the ventricles of the brain, raising intracranial pressure.
glossary.Vasogenic oedema: Brain swelling from leaky blood vessels, typical around tumours and responsive to steroids.
glossary.Cerebral oedema: Swelling of brain tissue from excess fluid.
glossary.Hypodense: Darker than normal brain on CT, as with oedema or many tumours.
glossary.Midline shift: Displacement of central brain structures to one side by a mass; a sign of dangerous pressure.
glossary.Lumbar puncture: A needle into the lower spinal canal to measure CSF pressure and sample the fluid.
glossary.LP: Lumbar puncture: needle sampling of CSF from the lower back, with opening pressure measured.
glossary.Opening pressure: The CSF pressure measured at the start of a lumbar puncture; raised in IIH.
glossary.Venous sinus thrombosis: A clot in the brain's draining venous sinuses, which can raise ICP and mimic IIH.
glossary.Venography: Imaging of veins; MR or CT venography shows the cerebral venous sinuses.
glossary.Mannitol: An osmotic diuretic given IV that draws water out of the brain to lower ICP.
glossary.Osmotic diuretic: A drug that stays in the blood and draws water out of tissues by osmosis, then is passed in urine.
glossary.Hypertonic saline: Concentrated salt solution given IV as an alternative osmotherapy to mannitol.
glossary.Dexamethasone: A potent corticosteroid used to reduce oedema around brain tumours.
glossary.Hyperventilation: Breathing faster or deeper than needed; on a ventilator it lowers CO2 to shrink cerebral blood volume.
glossary.PaCO2: Partial pressure of carbon dioxide in arterial blood; low values cause cerebral vasoconstriction.
glossary.GCS: Glasgow Coma Scale: scores eye, verbal and motor responses from 3 to 15.
glossary.ICP monitoring: A pressure sensor (bolt) placed in or on the brain on ICU to measure ICP continuously.
glossary.Lithium: A mood stabiliser for bipolar disorder; regular use is linked to idiopathic intracranial hypertension.
glossary.Metastasis: Cancer that has spread from its original site, such as lung cancer to the brain.

technique.stem: A 57 year old woman has a 4 week history of headaches that are worst when she wakes up and worse when she coughs. She has vomited most mornings this week. She had a mastectomy for breast cancer 3 years ago. Fundoscopy shows blurred optic disc margins in both eyes. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 150/86 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A headache diagnosis: look for red flags that point to a secondary cause.

clues: blurred optic disc margins in both eyes
steps.x: Morning headache worse on coughing, vomiting and **bilateral papilloedema**, in a woman with a cancer that spreads to brain.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Raised ICP**, probably from a cerebral metastasis.

elim: GCA: over 50 with jaw claudication and scalp tenderness; it does not cause papilloedema.
Medication overuse: daily headache with frequent analgesic use; no papilloedema.
Migraine: episodic, often with photophobia; normal discs.
Tension-type: band-like, no vomiting, normal fundi.

steps.x: **D. Raised intracranial pressure.** Rule: papilloedema + morning headache worse on coughing = raised ICP.

technique.stem: A 66 year old man is brought to the Emergency Department by his wife. He has had worsening headaches for 3 weeks and is now drowsy and confused. Fundoscopy shows bilateral papilloedema. He has no neck stiffness. His temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 58 bpm and BP 172/90 mmHg. His GCS is 12/15.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?

steps.x: 'Initial investigation' for a drowsy patient with signs of raised ICP.
Papilloedema, falling GCS and a slowing pulse with high BP: **raised ICP** until proven otherwise.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urgent CT head** to look for a SOL, bleed or hydrocephalus.

elim: EEG is for seizures; it does not show the cause of raised ICP.
LP before imaging can cause **coning**; contraindicated here.
MR venography is a second step after a normal CT.
Visual fields do not show the cause and waste time.

steps.x: **A. CT head.** Rule: suspected raised ICP = CT head first, never LP first.

technique.stem: A 24 year old man is brought to the Emergency Department after being hit on the head with a bottle. His GCS has fallen from 14/15 to 9/15 over the last hour. His left pupil is dilated. His pulse rate is 54 bpm and BP 184/88 mmHg. CT head shows a left extradural haematoma with midline shift. He is nursed 30 degrees head-up while theatre is prepared.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial pharmacological management?

steps.x: Pharmacological management while awaiting definitive surgery.

clues: pulse rate is 54 bpm and BP 184/88 mmHg
steps.x: Cushing's response and a blown pupil: severe raised ICP from a bleed, awaiting theatre.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV 20% mannitol** to buy time until decompression.

elim: Dexamethasone is for **tumour** oedema, not trauma or bleeds.
Furosemide is not the first-line osmotic agent for ICP.
The BP is protecting CPP; lowering it would worsen brain ischaemia.
Nimodipine prevents vasospasm after subarachnoid haemorrhage; it does not lower ICP.

steps.x: **D. Intravenous mannitol.** Rule: head up 30, then mannitol while awaiting theatre.

technique.stem: A 70 year old man has a large intracerebral haemorrhage. His GCS has fallen to 6/15. Over 30 minutes his BP rises from 150/80 mmHg to 210/90 mmHg and his pulse rate falls from 80 bpm to 44 bpm. His breathing becomes irregular.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his bradycardia?
o: Baroreceptor reflex response to a rise in blood pressure
Complete heart block from myocardial ischaemia
Direct vagal nerve compression in the neck

steps.x: A mechanism question: why does the pulse fall?

clues: BP rises from 150/80 mmHg to 210/90 mmHg
pulse rate falls from 80 bpm to 44 bpm
steps.x: Hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing = **Cushing's triad**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Rising ICP drops CPP, a sympathetic surge raises BP, and **baroreceptors** slow the heart.

elim: No beta-blocker is mentioned and it would not raise BP.
Heart block is not caused by the haemorrhage and does not explain the rising BP.
Nothing is compressing the neck; the problem is inside the skull.
No cold exposure; temperature is not given.

steps.x: **A. Baroreceptor reflex.** Rule: Cushing's bradycardia is a reflex response to the BP surge.

practice.stem: A 26 year old woman has a 2 month history of daily headaches that are worse when lying down, with brief episodes of blurred vision. Her BMI is 38 kg/m². Fundoscopy shows bilateral swollen optic discs. Neurological examination is otherwise normal. CT head is normal. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A young woman with a high BMI, headache, papilloedema and a normal CT has IIH. Optic neuritis is usually unilateral and painful on eye movement.

steps.x: Diagnosis of headache with visual symptoms.
Young, high BMI, postural headache, **papilloedema**, normal scan.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Possible but less likely with no clotting risk given; venography would be the next test to exclude it.
Migraine does not cause papilloedema.
Optic neuritis is usually unilateral with pain on eye movement and reduced acuity.
A pituitary adenoma gives bitemporal hemianopia and would show on imaging.

steps.x: **B. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension.** Rule: young + high BMI + papilloedema + normal CT.

practice.stem: A 59 year old man has a 3 week history of headaches on waking, worse when he bends over, and vomiting. He has small cell lung cancer. His pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 148/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on fundoscopy?
o: Cotton wool spots with flame haemorrhages
Swollen optic discs with blurred margins
practice.e: Raised ICP from a likely cerebral metastasis causes papilloedema: swollen discs with blurred margins.

steps.x: A finding on examination: what would raised ICP show at the disc?
Classic raised ICP headache in a patient likely to have **brain metastases**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Papilloedema**: bilateral swollen discs, blurred margins.

elim: Cherry-red spot is central retinal artery occlusion.
Cotton wool spots and flame haemorrhages are hypertensive or diabetic retinopathy.
Drusen are age-related macular degeneration.
Cupping is glaucoma.

steps.x: **E. Swollen optic discs with blurred margins.** Rule: raised ICP = papilloedema.

practice.stem: A 31 year old woman has a 6 week history of headaches and new double vision when looking to the right. Her BMI is 36 kg/m². Fundoscopy shows bilateral papilloedema. CT head is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on eye movement examination?
o: Failure of abduction of the right eye
Failure of adduction of the left eye with nystagmus of the right
Ptosis with a dilated right pupil
Right eye deviated down and out
Vertical diplopia on looking down and in
practice.e: Raised ICP stretches the abducens nerve: diplopia on looking right means the right lateral rectus fails, so the right eye cannot abduct.

steps.x: Eye movement finding in a patient with papilloedema.

clues: double vision when looking to the right
steps.x: IIH-type raised ICP with horizontal diplopia worst looking right.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Right CN VI palsy**: the right eye fails to abduct.

elim: That is internuclear ophthalmoplegia (MS), not raised ICP.
Ptosis with a dilated pupil is CN III (e.g. uncal herniation), not the classic sign here.
Down and out is CN III palsy.
Vertical diplopia looking down and in is CN IV.

steps.x: **A. Failure of abduction of the right eye.** Rule: raised ICP = CN VI false localising sign.

practice.stem: A 45 year old man is on the neurosurgical ward after a subdural haematoma. He becomes increasingly drowsy. His pulse rate is 46 bpm, BP 198/84 mmHg and respiratory rate 8 breaths per minute with irregular pauses. His GCS has fallen from 13/15 to 8/15.
practice.q: Which is the most likely explanation for his observations?
practice.e: Hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing with a falling GCS after a bleed is Cushing's triad of severely raised ICP.

steps.x: Explain the observations in a neurosurgical patient.
High BP, slow pulse, irregular breathing = **Cushing's triad**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Severely raised ICP** with impending herniation.

elim: Autonomic dysreflexia follows spinal cord injury above T6.
Hypertensive emergency does not explain bradycardia and irregular breathing after a bleed.
Neurogenic shock gives **hypotension** with bradycardia.
Opioids cause slow regular breathing and pinpoint pupils, with low or normal BP.

steps.x: **E. Severely raised ICP.** Rule: Cushing's triad = treat the brain, not the BP.

practice.stem: A 64 year old woman has a 2 week history of morning headaches, vomiting and a new left-sided weakness. She had a lobectomy for lung cancer 2 years ago. Fundoscopy shows bilateral papilloedema. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 72 bpm and BP 146/82 mmHg.
labs: Hypodense right parietal lesion with surrounding oedema
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her raised intracranial pressure?
practice.e: A hypodense lesion with surrounding oedema in a patient with previous lung cancer is a cerebral metastasis. An abscess would usually come with fever and a high CRP.

steps.x: Most likely cause of the raised ICP.
Raised ICP with a focal sign, previous lung cancer and no fever; the CT shows a hypodense lesion with oedema.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cerebral metastasis** from lung cancer.

elim: Abscess: fever and a markedly raised CRP; she is afebrile with CRP 6.
Hydrocephalus shows enlarged ventricles, not a parietal lesion.
Stroke is sudden, not 2 weeks of morning headache and papilloedema.
A subdural is a crescent of blood over the brain surface.

steps.x: **B. Cerebral metastasis.** Rule: hypodense lesion + oedema + known cancer = metastasis.

practice.stem: A 29 year old woman has a 1 month history of headaches and transient blurring of vision when she bends over. She has bipolar disorder. Fundoscopy shows bilateral papilloedema. CT head and MR venography are normal. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which of her medications is the most likely cause?
practice.e: Regular lithium use is a recognised cause of idiopathic intracranial hypertension. None of the other drugs causes raised ICP.

steps.x: A drug cause of raised ICP.

clues: CT head and MR venography are normal
steps.x: IIH picture (normal imaging) in a woman likely on a **mood stabiliser**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Lithium**-associated IIH.

elim: Amlodipine causes ankle oedema and flushing, not papilloedema.
Ibuprofen causes gastric and renal side effects, not raised ICP.
Omeprazole causes hypomagnesaemia, not raised ICP.
Sertraline causes hyponatraemia and GI upset, not papilloedema.

steps.x: **C. Lithium.** Rule: IIH risk = young woman, high BMI or lithium.

practice.stem: A 52 year old man has a 2 week history of progressive headache and is now confused. His wife says he vomited this morning. Fundoscopy shows bilateral papilloedema. There is no neck stiffness or rash. His temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 62 bpm and BP 166/94 mmHg. His GCS is 13/15.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: Papilloedema and a falling GCS mean raised ICP: urgent CT head first. LP before imaging risks coning.

steps.x: Initial investigation for suspected raised ICP.
Raised ICP signs, no meningism: find the cause quickly and safely.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urgent CT head**.

elim: Blood cultures are for sepsis; he is afebrile with no rash.
LP is contraindicated before CT with papilloedema.
MRI is more detailed but slower; it is not the urgent first test.
Visual fields do not find the cause.

steps.x: **D. Urgent CT head.** Rule: suspected raised ICP = CT before anything else.

practice.stem: A 23 year old woman has a 6 week history of headaches with bilateral papilloedema. Her BMI is 41 kg/m². Neurological examination is otherwise normal. CT head and MR venography are both normal.
practice.q: Which investigation will confirm the diagnosis?
practice.e: Once imaging excludes a lesion and venous sinus thrombosis, an LP showing raised opening pressure confirms IIH.

steps.x: Confirmatory (gold standard) test, after imaging.

clues: CT head and MR venography are both normal
steps.x: IIH suspected; imaging has made LP **safe** and excluded venous sinus thrombosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **LP with opening pressure**: raised CSF pressure confirms IIH.

elim: EEG is for seizures.
MRI spine does not assess intracranial pressure.
Repeating CT adds nothing after normal CT and venography.
Prolactin is for pituitary adenoma, which would show on imaging.

steps.x: **B. LP with opening pressure.** Rule: LP is the gold standard for CSF pressure, but only after imaging.

practice.stem: A 61 year old man has a 3 week history of morning headaches and drowsiness. He has metastatic melanoma. CT head shows two cerebral metastases with extensive surrounding oedema and no haemorrhage. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 152/88 mmHg. His GCS is 14/15.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial drug management?
practice.e: Raised ICP from tumour oedema is treated with high-dose IV dexamethasone, which reduces vasogenic oedema. Low-dose prednisolone is not adequate.

steps.x: Initial drug for raised ICP from metastases.
Malignancy-related raised ICP with **vasogenic oedema**, stable enough for drugs first.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **High-dose IV dexamethasone** + neurosurgical/oncology review.

elim: Aciclovir is for HSV encephalitis; no fever or temporal lobe change.
Levetiracetam treats seizures; he has not had one.
Acetazolamide is used in IIH, not tumour oedema.
5 mg prednisolone is far too weak for cerebral oedema.

steps.x: **A. High-dose IV dexamethasone.** Rule: tumour oedema = dexamethasone.

practice.stem: A 38 year old woman is in the Emergency Department after a fall down stairs. CT head shows a right subdural haematoma with midline shift. Her GCS is 11/15. Her pulse rate is 60 bpm and BP 170/90 mmHg. The neurosurgeon is on the way. She is lying flat on a trolley.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate step while awaiting the neurosurgeon?
o: Elevate the head of the bed to 30 degrees
Lie her in the left lateral position
practice.e: Head elevation to 30 degrees improves cerebral venous drainage and is the first step in raised ICP. Head-down tilt and LP worsen it.

steps.x: An immediate, simple step while waiting for surgery.

clues: pulse rate is 60 bpm and BP 170/90 mmHg
steps.x: Raised ICP from a bleed; she is flat, which impairs venous drainage.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Head up 30 degrees**.

elim: Left lateral is for airway or pregnancy positioning, not ICP.
LP with a mass and shift can cause coning.
Head-down tilt raises ICP.
The BP supports CPP; lowering it risks ischaemia.

steps.x: **A. Head up 30 degrees.** Rule: the first step in raised ICP is positioning.

practice.stem: A 50 year old man is intubated on the neurosurgical ICU after a traumatic brain injury. Despite head elevation and IV mannitol, his ICP rises to 35 mmHg and his right pupil becomes dilated. He is due in theatre in 20 minutes.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate temporary measure until surgery?
practice.e: Controlled hyperventilation lowers PaCO2, causing cerebral vasoconstriction and a rapid but short-lived fall in ICP: a bridge to theatre.

steps.x: A temporary rescue measure in severe raised ICP.

clues: Despite head elevation and IV mannitol
steps.x: First steps failed, herniation is starting and surgery is minutes away.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Controlled hyperventilation** as a bridge.

elim: High CO2 causes vasodilation and **raises** ICP.
Dexamethasone is not used for traumatic brain injury.
A lumbar drain with raised ICP risks coning.
Furosemide is not the rescue ICP treatment.

steps.x: **C. Controlled hyperventilation.** Rule: rapid, short-lived, reserved for emergencies.

practice.stem: A 47 year old woman with a large frontal meningioma is given an intravenous infusion of 20% mannitol while awaiting surgery. Over the next hour her ICP falls from 28 mmHg to 18 mmHg and her urine output rises.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism by which mannitol lowers her intracranial pressure?
o: Blocks carbonic anhydrase to reduce CSF production
Causes cerebral vasoconstriction by lowering PaCO2
Creates an osmotic gradient drawing water from brain into blood
Reduces capillary leak by stabilising the blood-brain barrier
Shrinks the tumour by inducing apoptosis
practice.e: Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic: it raises plasma osmolality, pulling water out of brain tissue into the circulation, then is excreted with water.

steps.x: Mechanism of mannitol.

clues: ICP falls from 28 mmHg to 18 mmHg
steps.x: An osmotic agent that lowers ICP and causes a diuresis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Osmotic gradient** draws water out of the brain into the vessels.

elim: That is acetazolamide.
That is hyperventilation.
That describes dexamethasone's effect on vasogenic oedema.
No drug here shrinks the tumour within an hour.

steps.x: **C. Osmotic gradient.** Rule: mannitol = water out; hyperventilation = blood volume down; dexamethasone = oedema down.
